title: TC1-05350
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): This is an appeal of an April 23, 2021 decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (Board) denying the Appellant's claim for refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c. 27 (IRPA).
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: This is an appeal of an April 23, 2021 decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (Board) denying the Appellant's claim for refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c. 27 (IRPA).

The Appellant, a Turkish national, claims that he fears persecution from the Turkish government due to i) his support of the Peoples' Democratic Party of Turkey (HDP) and ii) his status as a Kurdish member of the HDP.
For the reasons that follow, I deny this appeal.

The Appellant is a long-standing supporter of the HDP. His involvement with the Party was as follows: from time to time he visited the local HDP office; he attended election rallies; he contributed financially to the HDP; in 2015, he XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX for the Party; in XXXX 2018, he joined the HDP; during the June 2018 general elections, he again XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX for the Party and worked at an XXXX XXXX.

Shortly after the 2018 election, officers from a special operations unit ("gendarmes") advised the Appellant that they knew he was a member and supporter of the HDP. They warned him that if he did not stop supporting the Party, they would accuse him of selling illegal XXXX from the XXXX XXXX he owned with his father and brother. The gendarmes extorted money from him twice and regular police officers did so about ten times. In XXXX 2019, he closed the XXXX XXXX because of the extortion.

On XXXX XXXX, 2019, the gendarmes raided his home. They detained him for XXXX days and warned him that no matter where he went, they would find him and "get" him. When he was released, he was told not to engage in HDP activities or else he would be tortured. As a result, he decided to leave Turkey.

He came to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2019, travelling on a visitor visa he had obtained in 2016 in connection with a visit to his cousin who lives in Canada. He did not claim asylum upon arrival because he did not want to jeopardize his family's ability to visit him in Canada. On XXXX XXXX, 2019, his wife and two children joined him in Canada. On July 26, 2019, XXXX days after his family's return to Turkey, he signed his Basis of Claim form.

The Appellant seeks the admission of the following at appeal: 1) a XXXX XXXX, 2021 letter from his father confirming many of the facts relating to his claim and discussing the dismissal of Kurds from their jobs in Turkey; 2) a XXXX XXXX, 2021 letter from his brother confirming many of the facts relating to his claim and stating that, in Turkey, the police, the gendarmerie, the security forces, and the mafia are intertwined; and 3) a title deed to the family XXXX XXXX. The legal framework for the admission of evidence at appeal
paragraphs.heading_before: REQUEST FOR THE ADMISSION OF NEW EVIDENCE

paragraphs.text: Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA limits the admission of new evidence in an appeal before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to evidence that: 1) arose after the RPD's rejection of the claim; 2) was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim; or 3) an appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim. In addition, the Federal Court of Appeal held in the Singh case1-relying on its previous decision in Raza2-that the following factors must be met before new evidence could be admitted under subsection 110(4): newness, credibility, and relevance.3

The Appellant argues that there is yet another factor that I must consider in assessing the admissibility of the evidence he seeks to adduce at appeal. He relies on the Asri case,4 where Mr. Justice Russell held that while the RAD did not have to accept Mr. Arsi's explanation as to why the new evidence he attempted to adduce at appeal was not reasonably available before the rejection of the claim, if it did not, it may be obliged to consider "the severe consequences of not admitting [the] documentation."5 Mr. Justice Russell held that the RAD may be required, as part of its deliberations on admissibility, to ensure that was not refusing a genuine claim, thereby shocking the conscience of Canadians: The documentation was not disregarded as either irrelevant or because it was not genuine. Accordingly, there was a distinct possibility that the RAD was refusing a genuine claim because the Applicant had failed to convince it that these documents were not reasonably available earlier. In my view, this would shock the conscience of Canadians, who would expect the RAD to consider this possibility as a part of its deliberations on admissibility and, given what was at stake, consider some way of avoiding possible tragic consequence that did not require a disregard of the governing statutory provisions and the overall purpose of the IRPA which includes, inter alia, the protection of genuine refugees.6

Mr. Justice Russell's use of the word "Accordingly" in the passage above may suggest to some that he took the view that in all instances where the RAD found new evidence at appeal to be inadmissible based on a finding that documents were not reasonably available earlier as per subsection 110(4))-rather than based on a finding that they lacked relevance or genuineness as per Singh-there was "a distinct possibility that the RAD was refusing a genuine claim." However, I do not believe that he was making such a broad statement. I find that the additional requirement that the RAD would consider the conscience of Canadians-and "seek out" a way to consider the possibility that it might be refusing a genuine claim-as part of its deliberations on the admissibility of new evidence at appeal is limited to the circumstances of the Asri case, i.e., where the evidence the applicant sought the admission of was "likely conclusive support of the Applicant's refugee claim."7

Had Mr. Justice Russell intended to impose this additional requirement in all cases, he would have made this explicit. After all, such a requirement would be tantamount a reassessment of the findings in Singh and Raza, where the Federal Court of Appeal so carefully considered the issue of new evidence at appeal and, with Singh, the meaning of subsection 110(4). If the Federal Court of Appeal had intended to require the RAD to consider an additional, broadly applicable factor in assessing the application of subsection 110(4), surely it would have set this out in Singh.

Moreover, a broad obligation on the RAD to "seek out some way" of avoiding the possibility of rejecting a genuine claim by admitting evidence that does not meet the criteria of subsection 110(4) seems to require one of two approaches. One approach would be for the RAD to ignore the requirements of subsection 110(4). However, the Court of Appeal in Singh clearly ruled that the RAD was not vested with the discretion to disregard the conditions set out in subsection 110(4). It described the conditions of subsection 110(4), as "inescapable" and leaving "no room for discretion on the part of the RAD."8 It continued: [t]he admissibility of fresh evidence before the RAD is subject to strict criteria and neither the wording of the subsection nor the broader framework of the section it falls under could give the impression that Parliament intended to grant the RAD the discretion to disregard the conditions carefully set out therein.9

The Court of Appeal in Singh considered and rejected Madam Justice Gagné's (now Associate Chief Justice Gagné) reasoning in the Singh case at the Federal Court level,10 where she called for a flexible interpretation of subsection 110(4). It referred to her reasoning that a strict interpretation of subsection 110(4) would unfairly limit an applicant's access to a full fact-based appeal and that "the reduced timeframes within which claimants must submit their documents...support the flexible interpretation of the admissibility criteria."11 However, it concluded that these considerations did "not suffice to set aside the clear legislative intention to not authorize any new evidence on appeal other than in very specific and carefully defined circumstances."12

Another approach whereby the RAD might "seek out some way" of avoiding the possibility that it might reject a genuine claim because it found proposed new evidence to be inadmissible in accordance with subsection 110(4)-the approach suggested by the Appellant herein-would be by applying the conditions in that subsection with considerable flexibility. As the Appellant rightly notes, the Court of Appeal in Singh held that it went "without saying that the RAD always has the freedom to apply the conditions of subsection 110(4) with more or less flexibility depending on the circumstances of the case."13 However, a general requirement that the RAD apply the conditions of subsection 110(4) in the "flexible" way proposed by the Appellant would be tantamount to a requirement that it find that certain new evidence at appeal was not reasonably available before the rejection of the claim by the RPD whether or not it believed this to be the case as part of a duty to ensure that it did not reject a possible genuine claim (and in so doing, shock the conscience of Canadians). Such an approach would surely be ignoring the clear tests set out by the Parliament of Canada in subsection 110(4) and elaborated upon by the Federal Court of Appeal in its Singh/Raza analysis.

In sum, I find that the passage from Mr. Justice Russell was not intended to create a broadly applicable new approach to the admission of evidence at appeal, whereby the conscience of Canadians must become a factor in the RAD's assessment of the admissibility of documents that have not been found to lack relevance or genuineness. Instead, I find that Mr. Justice Russell intended to limit his finding to the circumstances of the Asri claim, i.e., where a finding that certain evidence the applicant sought the admission of at appeal was likely to provide conclusive support of the Applicant's refugee claim. In the instant case, the evidence the Appellant seeks the admission of does not meet this requirement. Letters from his father and brother

The Appellant argues that the two letters meet the first requirement of subsection 110(4) because they postdate the decision. This argument is, of course, without merit. As is well-known, it is not the case that, simply because an item of proposed new evidence is dated after the rejection of the claim, it "arose" after that rejection for the purposes of the first requirement of subsection 110(4). In the Raza case-on which the Appellant relies-the Federal Court of Appeal made clear that the newness of documentary evidence cannot be tested solely by the date on which the document was created: "[w]hat is important is the event or circumstance sought to be proved by the documentary evidence."14 The information provided in the letters did not arise after the rejection of the claim; instead the information represents a restatement of the story the Appellant gave to the RPD. The only possible exception to this are the comments from his brother and father about the treatment of Kurds by the Turkish government. However, without any indication from the letters' authors that this treatment arose after the rejection of his claim, I am not in a position to find that it did.

In addition, the Appellant argues that the letters meet subsection 110(4) because he was not aware that he needed to provide supporting evidence from his family members. He argues that, given that he believed the evidence that he did provide on the subject of his HDP affiliations-a XXXX XXXX, 2020 letter from the HDP Provincial President in the XXXX XXXX district-was adequate, and given his limited education, his lack of awareness was reasonable. While he was represented by counsel, he argues that that representation should not be used as "a catch-all way" to reject his explanation. He relies on the Federal Court of Appeal's observation in Singh, discussed above, that the RAD "always has the freedom to apply the condition of subsection 110(4) with more or less flexibility depending on the circumstances of the case."

The question becomes whether the circumstances of this case are such that I should apply the requirements of subsection 110(4) flexibly and, if so, whether that would result in my finding that the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected to have submitted the letters before the rejection of the claim. In deciding on that question, I am guided by the following finding by the Federal Court of Appeal-also in Singh-in relation to the RAD's application of subsection 110(4): "The role of the RAD is not to provide the opportunity to complete a deficient record submitted before the RPD...".15 The Federal Court in the Eshetie case elaborated: [33] It is important to bear in mind that an analysis of the admissibility of new evidence before the RAD begins with the premise that the appeal of an RPD decision is intended to be a paper-based appeal [Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Singh, 2016 FCA 96 (CanLII), [2016] 4 FCR 230] at paras 35, 51). A RAD appeal is not a second chance to submit evidence to answer weaknesses identified by the RPD (Abdullahi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 260 at para 15): [15] In other words, responding to an inadequacy identified by the RPD in a party's case cannot be a legitimate foundation for the party to claim that had she known about the deficiency she could have presented better evidence that was always in existence from persons that could have been called, in this case from her cousin. This would make the RPD process a monumental waste of time, which is surely not Parliament's intention in providing appeal rights. [34] An applicant is required to put his or her best foot forward to the RPD. In this case, a great deal of the new evidence submitted by the Applicant could and should have been provided to the RPD.16

In view of the jurisprudence and, given that the Appellant was represented by experienced counsel, I find that he would have (or should have) known of the importance of providing supporting evidence about his link to the Party-the issue at the very heart of this claim. The extent of his education is of little relevance. He was not relying on his personal knowledge of refugee law or procedure; rather, he had the benefit of expert legal advice. While it is true that he did provide a single document meant to show his link to the Party, his counsel would (or should) have been aware of the risk of operating on the assumption that a single piece of evidence was all that was required. This is especially so in view of the content of the letter. As discussed in my analysis below, the XXXX XXXX, 2020 letter is short, impersonal, and attributes activities to the Appellant that do not correspond with his testimony, while failing to mention activities that he claims to have performed.

While there may be instances where a represented claimant may be justifiably surprised by the level of proof demanded by an RPD decision-maker,17 this is not such a case. It is not a case where the evidence provided by the Appellant was so very persuasive that it would be unreasonable to have expected the Appellant (or his counsel) to have adduced additional evidence at his RPD hearing.

The two letters do not meet the requirements of subsection 110(4). As such, I need not consider whether they comply with the factors outlined in Singh. They are inadmissible. Title deed for the XXXX XXXX

Once again, the Appellant argues that he could not reasonably have been expected to have provided the title document showing that his family owns a XXXX XXXX because he did not think he needed to. Once again, he points to his limited education and the fact that he submitted a letter from the HDP.

For the reasons discussed above-including that he is ably represented-his claim that he did not know about the need to prove ownership of the XXXX is not reasonable. After all, his co-ownership of the XXXX XXXX is interconnected with his overall claim: it was linked to the alleged threats from the gendarmes (i.e., they threatened to spread rumours that he was selling illegal XXXX); the claimed extortion money was paid from his family's XXXX XXXX funds; and it was shortly after he shut down the XXXX XXXX that the authorities allegedly raided his home-"'you thought that you would avoid us by closing your XXXX XXXX'"18-detained him, and threatened to torture him. That he provided supporting evidence about his link to the HDP does nothing support his claim that he did not know that he needed to provide evidence that his family owned a XXXX XXXX; to the contrary, it undermines that claim by showing that he was indeed aware of the importance of providing supporting evidence in a refugee claim.
The title document does not meet the requirements of subsection 110(4) and, as such, is inadmissible.
Because no new evidence has been admitted, the request for a hearing pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA must be denied.
The determinative issue in this case is credibility.
In my review of the RPD's decision, I will apply a standard of correctness.19 This is not a case where the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage in making its findings.20 ANALYSIS

The RPD held 1) based on problems with his credibility, including the provision of inadequate supporting evidence, that the Appellant was not a long-standing supporter of the Party, he had not engaged in the activities in support of the Party he claimed to have, and he was not extorted or detained by the Turkish authorities based on his involvement with the Party. Consequently, it held that he did not face risk on that basis upon return. In addition, it held 2) that, while he was a member of the HDP as of XXXX 2020, that membership, in conjunction with his Kurdish ethnicity, did not place him at risk. Finally, it held 3) that his status as a Kurd would not lead to a serious possibility of persecution or a likelihood of other harm.

The Appellant contests the RPD's findings that he was not at risk because 1) of his involvement with the HDP or 2) of his status as a Kurdish member of the HDP. However, he does not contest its finding 3) that his Kurdish ethnicity alone would not lead to a serious possibility of persecution or a likelihood of other harm.

I have reviewed the RPD's uncontested finding that he does not face a serious possibility of persecution or a likelihood of other harm in Turkey due to his Kurdish ethnicity alone and I agree with it. As it is uncontested, I will not discuss it further. I. Is the Appellant at risk because of his work with the HDP? Credibility: Knowledge of the HDP and fairness RPD's findings

The RPD held that the Appellant's knowledge of the HDP was not commensurate with his claimed long-term involvement with the Party. He lacked the ability to speak about the HDP's policies and his testimony on the subject was vague and brief. It noted that when asked about HDP policies, he simply said that it supported peace, democracy, and equality. He provided no detail whatsoever about the policies and platforms advocated by the HDP. It considered that the Appellant had not completed high school; however, it did not find that this explained his lack of knowledge. It held that he should have been able to provide detailed testimony, without prompting, about the HDP, including that it is a socialist and secular party which advocates for democracy, women's and minorities' rights, and is anti-capitalist and pro-worker. While it acknowledged that the Appellant did have some knowledge of the Party (he knew the names of the two current leaders of the Party and the year it was formed), it nevertheless found his knowledge deficient. Appellant's arguments

The Appellant argues that the RPD's expectations were too high; his answers were consistent with what could reasonably be expected of a "rank-and-file supporter" with a limited education. His loyalty to the Party may reasonably be explained by his family's long-term support of pro-Kurdish parties for decades, and/or the loyalty a Kurd might reasonably have to a Party devoted to Kurdish people's freedom. He also argues that the RPD failed to give his knowledge of the Party (as noted, he knew the names of the two current leaders of the Party and the year it was formed) adequate weight in reaching its finding.

In addition, he argues that the RPD acted unfairly because it faulted him for i) not knowing about the Party's views on economic matters, when he was not even questioned about them and ii) not stating that the HDP was anti-capitalist, when its source for its statement that it was anti-capitalise was an article that was a) not disclosed to the Appellant and b) from Wikipedia, an unreliable source. My analysis

Knowledge of the HDP. There is a certain tension in this claim. On the one hand, the Appellant's claim is based on him having been so involved with the HDP that the Turkish authorities came to know of his support and want to harm him because of it. At the same time, in view of his superficial testimony about the Party, he now argues that he is a mere "rank and file" supporter of the HDP-a Party that has some six million supporters who voted for it in the 2018 election and an estimated 40,000 members21-and it is unreasonable to expect him to know very much about the it, aside from that it is pro-Kurd and focussed on fairness and equality.

The Appellant's testimony about why he supports the Party and what he believes it stands for was very shallow indeed. He was unable to testify that the HDP was anything other than a party that supports the Kurdish people's freedom, peace, and democracy; "is on the side of equality;" and is not a religious party. There may be cases, of course, where a voter or even a member of a party, would reasonably have a limited understanding of a party's policies and/or may have joined a party based on a very general view that it was friendly to their ethnic group, in favour of equality, or because their family has supported it. However, I do not accept that someone who had the level of involvement with the HDP the Appellant claims he did would have such a limited knowledge of its policies. It is highly unlikely that the Party would entrust someone to publicly represent it-by working at an XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX-if that person was so lacking in knowledge that they were unable to provide even the most basic details about party policy, beyond its favourable view of Kurdish rights and a focus on equity and justice.

Moreover, the Appellant's limited knowledge of the Party is incompatible with his claim that, if he returned to Turkey, he would "continue to involve [him]self in pro-Kurdish politics, as this is a crucial expression of my political opinion and identity."22 I find that it is highly unlikely that someone who feels so strongly about pro-Kurdish politics that he would be willing to risk his life in order to continue to be involved in such politics-despite having been extorted, detained, and threatened with torture in the past and despite believing he will be subjected to cruel and unusual treatment, including possibly torture, in the future-would know so little about the cause he is willing to risk so much to champion.

Fairness. As to the Appellant's first fairness argument, while it is true that the RPD did not ask him about the HHDP's economic policies, I can see no reason why fairness would have required that it did so. It asked the Appellant, in an open-ended way, what policies the HDP supported and I can see no reason why he could not have spoken about their economic policies, among other things. I do not find it was unfair for the RPD to have had regard to his lack of knowledge of the HDP's policies on economic matters.

More troubling, however, is the Appellant's second fairness argument. The law on the use of specialized knowledge by an RPD decision-maker is set out at paragraph 170(i) of the IRPA, which provides that the RPD "may take notice of any facts that may be judicially noticed, any other generally recognized facts and any information or opinion that is within its specialized knowledge." Rule 22 of the RPD Rules23 limits the RPD's reliance on specialized knowledge: Before using any information or opinion that is within its specialized knowledge, the Division must notify the claimant or protected person and, if the Minister is present at the hearing, the Minister, and give them an opportunity to (a) make representations on the reliability and use of the information or opinion; and (b) provide evidence in support of their representations.

The RPD's reliance on evidence that was not before the Appellant means that there has, ipso facto, been a breach of procedural fairness. This was made clear by Madam Justice Tremblay-Lamer in N'Sungani:24 [21] The Board, by virtue of its own rules, is required to give notice to the parties prior to utilizing any information or opinion that is within its specialized knowledge...in order to give them an opportunity to respond. Failure to do so constitutes a breach of procedural fairness. In Gonzalez v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1981] 2 F.C. 781 at 782 (C.A.), quoted in Hu v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2003] F.C.J. No. 788 at para. 25 (T.D.)(QL), Urie J.A. described what sort of information constitutes specialized knowledge: The information was not the sort of information of which judicial notice could be taken in proceedings before a court nor was it or the general character well known to the Board and to the public referred to in the Maslej case [Maslej v. Minister of Manpower and Immigration, [1977] 1 F.C. 194 (C.A.)]. If the kind of information used in this case, which appears to be of a type which an applicant might well be in a position to contest, is to be relied upon by the Board in a hearing...natural justice requires that the applicant be entitled to respond to it just as he would to evidence adduced at the hearing. [emphasis added] Similarly, in the Kirichenko case,25 where the RPD relied on a document that was not available to the claimant and whose contents were unclear, Mr. Justice Russell found a breach of procedural fairness, noting that "the Applicant was given no opportunity to address at least one of the sources for the RPD's finding on" a matter which was "the central focus of this application."26

The question then becomes what the appropriate remedy is for the RPD's breach of natural justice. Madam Justice Tremblay-Lamer held in N'Sungani that, while voiding the decision is the rule, an exception exists: Ordinarily, a breach of procedural fairness voids the hearing and the resulting decision but an exception to this rule exists...This exception stems from Mobil Oil Canada Ltd. v. Canada-Newfoundland Offshore Petroleum Board, [1987 CanLII 5074 (NL SC)]...where the Supreme Court of Canada explained that a breach of procedural fairness does not require a new hearing in "special circumstances" where the claim in question is otherwise "hopeless" or the outcome reached was "inevitable"....27 In Mir, Mr. Justice Kelen made clear that the procedural error in that case did not, in the circumstances, necessitate setting the decision aside because, even if the applicant had had the chance to respond, it would not have impacted the final decision.28

Unlike in N'Sungani-or indeed in Mir-where the procedural error was found by a court charged with judicial review, I have found a procedural error in circumstances where I am charted with providing a de novo assessment of the claim. While I have found a breach of procedural fairness arising from the RPD's reliance on its specialized knowledge in contravention of Rule 22, I will not have regard to the Wikipedia article in my reassessment of the Appellant's credibility. As such, the RPD's error will have no impact on my reassessment and there is no need to set the RPD's decision aside. For the same reason, I do not need to decide on whether Wikipedia is a reliable source; however, I note that the Federal Court case law suggests that it is not the sort of evidence the Board normally should rely on,29 despite the Board's relatively informal approach to the evidentiary rules. Conclusion

In view of the foregoing, I draw a negative credibility finding based on the Appellant's limited knowledge of the HDP in the circumstances. In making this finding, I have had regard to his limited education and to the fact that he was able to give some limited information about the HDP. Credibility: Lack of reasonably available supporting evidence RPD's findings

The RPD drew a series of negative credibility findings based on the Appellant's failure to make reasonable attempts to procure supporting evidence that should have been reasonably available. It noted the lack of supporting evidence: 1) showing that he supported the HDP financially (the Appellant explained that he had not asked for a receipt but he gave no explanation as to why he had not sought receipts at a later point, i.e., while in Canada);30 2) from his family members who could attest to his support for the HDP (the RPD rejected his explanations that he did not think about it or see the need, noting that he was well-represented and had regular contact with his family); 3) from other HDP members or volunteers to confirm his activities for the Party (when asked why he had not made efforts, he provided no explanation, other than noting that he had submitted a letter from the HDP); 4) to support his claim that he had paid extortion money ten to twelve times, e.g. bank records; 5) to show that the XXXX XXXX was closed or that he and his family owned a XXXX XXXX; or 6) to support the XXXX 2019 raid on his home or his two-day detention. Appellant's arguments

First, the Appellant argues that he was unable to provide receipts of his donations to the HDP because he did not ask for them. Second, he argues that he had no reason to adduce more supporting evidence to show his involvement with the HDP because his letter from the HDP was arguably the "best possible evidence."31 Finally, he relies on the letters from his father and brother as new evidence at appeal.

Because the Appellant does not contest the RPD's findings regarding the lack of documents discussed at items 4)-6) above, I will not address these findings in this decision. I note, however, that I have considered the RPD's reasoning and agree with it. Legal framework

My negative credibility finding based on the Appellant's limited knowledge of the HDP means that he has lost the benefit of the Maldonado presumption that his sworn evidence is truthful.32 Consequently, I need not consider the interplay between his obligation to prove his claim, as per RPD Rule 11,33 and the Maldonado presumption. The Federal Court recognized that it is an error to make an adverse credibility finding on the basis of the absence of corroborative evidence unless 1) there is a valid reason to doubt the claimant's credibility or 2) the decision-maker does not accept the claimant's explanation for failing to produce such evidence when it would be reasonably expected to be available.34 My analysis

First, I accept that the Appellant's explanation that he did not ask for receipts is reasonable as far as it goes. It is perfectly plausible that someone might donate to a political party and not ask for receipts. However, the RPD's concern was focussed on the fact that the Appellant made no efforts to obtain receipts showing his donations to the party after the fact-i.e. after he came to Canada and pursued a refugee claim-and provided no reasonable explanation why. Given that donation receipts are available according to the country condition evidence,35 I find that his failure to explain why he opted not to obtain them warrants a negative credibility finding.

Second, the Appellant's claim that a letter from the HDP is more probative than a letter from his family members or his fellow HDP volunteers might be true if the letter directly corresponded with his evidence, was personalized in nature, and was more detailed. As discussed below, that is not the case with the letter he provided. Moreover, even if a letter from the Party is highly probative or the "best possible evidence" of the Appellant's links to the HDP, it does not necessarily follow that the Board's expectation that there would be more supporting evidence was incorrect. It is certainly not unusual for the RPD to expect, and for a claimant to provide, more than a single item of objective proof on an issue, in particular one that is at the very heart of a claim-in this case, a connection to the HDP that the Appellant claims has led to his detention and may in the future lead to persecution or other harm.
Finally, I note that I have found the letters from the Appellant's brother and father inadmissible above. I cannot, of course, consider inadmissible evidence.

In view of the nature of the letter that the Appellant provided and the importance of proving his claim, including that he was affiliated with the HDP, I agree that the RPD was correct to expect there be more supporting evidence. As discussed above in my assessment of the new evidence the Appellant proposed at appeal, it falls to a claimant-in particular one who is represented but experienced counsel-to provide sufficient evidence to prove their claim. Letter from the HDP RPD's findings

The RPD placed little weight on the XXXX XXXX, 2020 supporting letter from the HDP-the sole supporting document linking him to the HDP-noting that it was silent regarding his claim to have been a long-standing HDP supporter with who undertook certain important functions such as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. It noted that the description of the Appellant's contributions in the letter-that he had worked in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX-did not jibe with his evidence, i.e., that that he engaged in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, provided financial donations, and worked at a XXXX XXXX. It noted further that he made no mention in his evidence of his having participated in congresses or exhibitions. The RPD also noted that the letter appeared to be a template and had no personal details. Appellant's arguments

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in finding that the HDP letter warranted little weight because i) it erred by dismissing supporting evidence because of what it does not say, rather than considering it for what it does say; ii) even if it is a template, it does not mean that it is not largely accurate or that it does not largely apply to the Appellant; iii) it was being microscopic-after all, "congresses" and "exhibition" are broad enough that they could include attending meetings at the HDP office or volunteering at an XXXX XXXX; and iv) the letter was sufficient to prove to the RPD's satisfaction that he was a member of the Party-which, as he argues below, is all that is necessary for his claim to succeed. My analysis

I will consider the Appellant's arguments one-by-one: i) The RPD did not reject the letter because of what it did not say. Instead, it found that it warranted less weight as evidence to support the Appellant's claim that he had a strong affiliation with the HDP, given that it was not personalized and its description of the work undertaken by the Appellant did not fully jibe with the Appellant's evidence (see iii) below). Indeed, it specifically accepted that it proved that he was a member-though it noted that it did not state when he became one. As Mr. Justice Grammond held in Adeleye, the prohibition on discounting evidence for what it does not say-i.e. disbelieving one witness's evidence simply because another witness corroborated only part of that evidence and remained silent as to another part-"does not detract from the general requirement that there be sufficient evidence to ground a finding of a well-founded fear of persecution."36 ii) I agree with the Appellant that just because a letter is based on a template it does not mean that its contents are not accurate. However, that was not the point being made by the RPD. Its point was that a letter, such as this one, which has little or no personalized detail about a member of a political party, is less probative than a letter that described the specific contribution of the claimant in a personalized way-and did so in a way that jibed with the story told by the claimant (see iii) below). I agree. iii) In this case, the letter from the HDP does not correspond with the Appellant's evidence in two ways: first, it fails to include contributions that the Appellant claims to have made (XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, volunteering at a XXXX, and donating funds) and second, it includes contributions that the Appellant does not mention in his evidence (attendance at congresses and exhibitions). I can see no basis upon which a close examination of the only evidence supporting the Appellant's link to the HDP, in order to determine if it supports his claims, may be characterized as microscopic. His contributions-and the alleged repercussions arising therefrom-are the reason for the claim and it is by no means overly demanding to expect that his evidence and that of the Party will refer to similar contributions. In circumstances where the Appellant had more than one document to support his claimed connection to the HDP, it may well be that a detailed comparison between the support letter and his evidence would not be required. However, this is not such a case. I disagree that the letter's reference to attendance at "congresses" or "exhibitions" may be read to include the Appellant's claim to have visited at the HDP headquarters and to have volunteered at XXXX XXXX. It is not inconceivable, of course, that there could have been a XXXX at an HDP congress or exhibition; however, it is certainly not something that one would presume-even when affording the benefit of the doubt to the Appellant. Moreover, even if I were to speculate that, in using the terms congresses or exhibitions, the letter's author was referring to the Appellant's claimed attendance at the party headquarters or his having worked at a XXXX, the fact remains that the Appellant's claims to have donated to the party and engaged in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX were not mentioned in the letter. In addition, the letter is silent on the issue of whether or not the Appellant became a member of the HDP in 2018 as he claims. It does not state when he became a Party member-only that he was "still a member" in XXXX 2020 when the letter was written. Nor does it indicate over what period he worked as a supporter the Party. iv) Finally, the Appellant is correct that the letter provides that he was, as of XXXX XXXX, 2020, when the letter was written, a member of the HDP-and correct that this was something that the RPD accepted as true. However, as I will discuss below, I do not share this view.

I accept the letter from the HDP has probative value. Having said that, the letter is of less value that it would otherwise be because it is general in nature, it does not elaborate on the length of time he has been a member of or associated with the Party, and some of the activities it states that the Appellant engaged in he did not mention in his evidence and other activities he claims to have engaged in are not mentioned in the letter. Conclusion on his credibility

When I weigh the above credibility concerns alongside the Appellant's extraordinarily limited supporting evidence-in addition to the HDP letter discussed above, the only personal supporting evidence he provided was a letter from a Kurdish organization in Toronto stating that he is of Kurdish descent-I find that he is lacking in credibility. I find that the letter from the HDP does not outweigh my credibility concerns. As such, I find that the Appellant was not a member of the HDP, did not assist the Party, was not pursued by the Turkish authorities based on his actual or perceived political opinion, was not extorted by the Turkish authorities, and was not detained or threatened with torture. Consequently, I find that he does not face a serious possibility of persecution on the basis of his political affiliation (or perceived political affiliation); nor does he face a likelihood of harm as per subsection 97(1). Conclusion on the sufficiency of evidence

In addition, having regard to the limited evidence that has been provided and the Appellant's loss of the Maldonado presumption, I find that he has not met his burden of proving that he faces a serious possibility of persecution on the basis of his past political affiliation (or perceived political affiliation); nor has he shown that he faces a likelihood of harm as per subsection 97(1).37 Is the Appellant a Convention refugee based on his status as a Kurdish HDP supporter?

The Appellant argues i) that even if I doubt his specific allegations, the country condition evidence shows that active HDP supporters or members are at risk of persecution if they voice their political opinion openly; and ii) that there is no guarantee that the Turkish authorities will not ban the HDP altogether and, if it does so, there is no guarantee that he will not be at risk of persecution solely on the basis that he was a member of the Party.

Once again, I disagree. While I accept that he has proven that he is Kurdish, as noted above, I have found that he was not a member of the HDP and that he did not assist the Party. Consequently, I need not consider how a person who was an HDP member or supporter would be treated-whether that person is Kurdish or not.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, I confirm the decision of the RPD. The appeal is dismissed.
